1:
Whether this is a psalm at all, or the tail of the one before it, is contested. Adam Clarke counts the witnesses for joining them: eighteen manuscripts of one collator and fifty-three of another, some ancient editions, the Septuagint, the Syriac, the Vulgate, the Arabic and the Anglo-Saxon, and an old Anglo-Scottish Psalter that reads it straight on from the foregoing. Keil and Delitzsch report the same versions and refuse them: this psalm has scarcely anything in common with its predecessor except one phrase, the arrangement is arbitrary and condemns itself, though a Jewish commentator favoured it and it has found admission into not a few Hebrew manuscripts. The paragraph attached to John Calvin’s block leans the other way, calling the opinion that it is only a continuation of the former not improbable, since the earlier psalm ended abruptly and the ejaculations here arise so naturally from what was just recited.

Who wrote it, and when, produces a scatter of guesses. That same paragraph stacks them: one refers it to a passage of Chronicles, some suppose it written by Moses at the Red Sea, others by David in the beginning of his reign, others by Mordecai and Esther, others by the three children in the fiery furnace, perhaps by Hezekiah or someone in the Babylonish captivity; and a further writer, while allowing that nothing certain can be concluded, conjectures the time of Hezekiah and the deliverance from the blasphemies and arrogance of Sennacherib. Calvin himself will say only that it was penned when the Church was deeply afflicted. Clarke likewise says the author is unknown and the occasion unknown, and calls it a triumphal song in which the victory gained is entirely ascribed to God. Keil and Delitzsch guess an expedition against heathen enemies, and pass on a pleasing conjecture that the sacrifice proceeded while the psalm was sung, a priest’s voice proclaiming its acceptance partway through, though they place the change of voices earlier than that. C.H. Spurgeon fixes on its use rather than its origin, that it was sung at the Passover and so bears relation to the deliverance from Egypt.

The taunt in the second verse is felt most sharply by Charles Ellicott, who says it is difficult for us to reproduce in imagination the apparent triumph which the idolater, able to point to his deity, felt over the worshipper of the invisible God when outward events seemed to be going against him. Spurgeon presses the same point into the present: God may not work miracles at the beck and call of every boaster who challenges him, and those who once bade his Son come down from the cross would now have him overstep the ordinary bounds of providence to convince them. Augustine of Hippo takes the answer strictly, that he is not in the heaven where men see the sun and moon and adore them, but in a heaven above all bodies; nor is he there in such a sense as to dread a fall should heaven be withdrawn from under him. Matthew Henry hears in the opening line that boasting is for ever excluded, and that all our crowns must be cast at the feet of him who sits upon the throne. Clarke reads the third verse as a confession, that there was too much cause for his abandoning them to their enemies. John Gill gives the heathen a contemporary face, applying the reproach to the Papists of his own day.
4:
The catalogue is taken as a real anatomy. Keil and Delitzsch call the carved gods dead images devoid of all life, even of the sensuous life whose outward organs are imagined upon them, and pause over the grammar of the middle verses, where the words for their hands and their feet are either subjects rendered prominent by the construction or absolute cases, since the idols themselves are the subjects of both verbs. Charles Ellicott sharpens the last clause of the list, that the Hebrew implies not only the want of articulate speech but of utterance at all. John Gill goes through the members one by one against the God who has none of them: the idols are carved with mouths but make no use of them, and if any cry to them they cannot answer or save, whereas the God in the heavens answers his people and tells them his grace is sufficient; their makers took care to set a pair of ears on their heads but could not convey the faculty of hearing, so that priests may cry from morning to noon and nothing is heard; they have hands but cannot stretch them out to receive anything from their worshippers or give anything to them.

Two of them show that the ancients themselves saw the joke. Adam Clarke observes that idolatry was so obviously vain that the more serious heathens ridiculed it and made it a butt for the jests of their freethinkers and buffoons, and he quotes a satirist asking whether the god hears, and why he does not move his lips when he ought to speak out, whether he is of marble or of bronze, and why men lay incense and the liver of a calf on his altar, since as far as the poet can discern there is no difference between the god’s statue and that of a certain musician — the point being sharper, Clarke adds, because that musician was a player whose image had been set up by a tyrant’s order in a temple. Gill supplies the counterpart from the other side: the image of one god in Crete was made without ears at all, because it was thought unbecoming that he who was prince and lord of all should give ear to any.

The closing line divides on its mood. Gill takes it first as a statement, that the makers are as stupid and senseless as the matter they work in, but reports that two Jewish commentators read it as a petition, let them that make them be like unto them, and that the ancient versions do the same, so that what looks like a description becomes an imprecation. Ellicott ends with a couplet drawing the same distinction between maker and worshipper, that whoever moulds a sacred face in gold or stone does not make the god, but he who asks his grace does. Gill also refuses to leave the idols in antiquity, applying the whole description twice over to the images of the Papists of his own day.
9:
The third of the three groups addressed is identified four different ways. John Gill insists the phrase is not meant to sort true saints from hypocrites within the other two, but to describe people belonging to neither, and he cites two Jewish commentators for God-fearers of every people and nation, that is, proselytes. John Wesley says the same in a line, all who worship the true God, not only Israelites but even Gentile proselytes. Matthew Henry agrees, the proselytes who are not of the seed of Israel but worship him and make conscience of their duty. Adam Clarke drops the ethnic question altogether and reads it of all real penitents and sincere believers. Charles Ellicott takes the opposite line from all of them in five words, glossing the same phrase as all Israel.

The abrupt turn from confession to address is explained two ways. Ellicott finds consummate art in it, like the pointed application of a general truth in a sermon, and reconstructs the performance: it is possible that a change in the music was made here, the choir turning to the people with a loud burst of song, one part of the choir or one officiating priest charging the whole congregation in turn to trust, with the full choir taking up the refrain each time and repeating back to him the ground on which he urged confidence, until at the next verses congregation and choir join and change to the first person. C.H. Spurgeon accounts for the same shift of person psychologically instead: in using the word their the psalmist may have been speaking to himself in a sort of soliloquy, whispering after his own exhortation that they may well trust, since God is at all times the strength of his servants. Keil and Delitzsch mark the point where the voice of consolation begins, and note that it becomes a voice of hope by being blended with the newly strengthened believing tone of the congregation.

That fear and trust are not rivals is argued by two of them. Gill says faith and fear are consistent, and that where there is holy reverence and godly fear, neither slavish nor hypocritical, there will also be confidence; he instances a man famous for fearing God who nonetheless trusted him. Henry puts it as a rule, that wherever there is an awful fear of God there may be a cheerful faith in him, since those who reverence his word may rely upon it. On the second group they converge with a common motive. Spurgeon tells the priests that those nearest to him should trust him most, since their very calling is bound up with his truth, and adds that it is good to exhort to faith those who already have it. Henry observes that they are the most maligned and struck at by the enemies and therefore the objects of particular care, and ought to be examples of confidence in the worst of times. Gill extends the office forward, since under the Gospel all the saints are priests, whose sacrifices cannot please God without faith. Clarke, who takes the house of Aaron simply as the different classes of the priesthood, gives the blessing section a literal rendering of his own and points out how many of its words are redoubled to make the subject more affecting.
14:
The division of heaven and earth is read four ways. Keil and Delitzsch take it historically: God has reserved the heavens to himself but given the earth to men, and this separation is a fundamental characteristic of the history that follows the flood. John Wesley reads it as a claim of title, since the previous verse declares God the creator of both and this one asserts that he is their Lord and governor to dispose of all men and things as he pleases. Adam Clarke makes it a grant dated from the expulsion from paradise, when God turned man out into the earth and gave it to him and his sons for ever, that they might dress and till it and eat of its produce all their days. C.H. Spurgeon offers two senses and will not choose between them. On the first, the world has been left in great measure under the power and will of men, so that things below are not in the same perfect order as things above; the free agency God gave his creatures required that he should in some degree restrain his own power and suffer men to follow their own devices, though since he has not vacated heaven he remains master of earth and can at any time gather all the reins into his own hands. On the second, the clause is a reason for the increase just promised, since God gave the earth to his people and intends that they shall fill it, man having been made his deputy over the world.

The line about the dead is narrowed by everyone who touches it. Clarke restricts it to the idolaters of the earlier verses, those dead men who worshipped dumb idols as gods and dying in their sins do not worship God at all. John Gill narrows it twice, excluding both the dead in sin and the departed saints, whose souls do not sleep but praise God continually with the angels, and who are barred only from praising him with the bodily organs death has made useless until the resurrection. Spurgeon keeps it entirely to this world: the preacher cannot magnify the Lord from his coffin, the tomb sends forth no voice, and one by one the singers in the consecrated choir steal away and we miss their music, so that those left have need to sing the more earnestly. Charles Ellicott simply names the place, that the land of silence is the under-world. Wesley calls it the grave.

On the word used in the older English versions Clarke turns philologist. He reports an Aramaic paraphrase that renders the phrase as the house of earthly sepulture, quotes two old English renderings that both put hell where the newer versions have silence, and defuses them by etymology: among our ancestors the word meant originally the covered or hidden obscure place, from a verb to cover or conceal, and only later came to express the place of endless torment. His own close is a prayer that the fathers who received so much are dead and silent in the grave, that the living stand in their place and wish to magnify the name, and that further blessings be granted before they die so that they may praise as living monuments of mercy. Spurgeon ends by refusing every excuse for silence, since neither affliction nor old age nor death itself shall damp the fires, and even if no miracle is worked now they will praise on the strength of what was done in ages past. Ellicott renders the promise of increase more literally as a heaping of blessings on them and on their children.
